c.tagline: Faded colonial charm at the gateway to the Bijagós Islands.

taxi.fareNote: Shared 'town taxis' run fixed routes with fixed per-seat fares (roughly 300-600 CFA); private hire or airport trips are negotiated in cash beforehand since meters aren't used.

emergency.note: Emergency response is very limited nationwide and medical facilities are basic; contact your embassy and travel-insurance assistance line for serious problems.

hood_landmark.Bissau Velho (Old Town): Fortaleza de São José da Amura, Bissau

hood_desc: The weathered Portuguese colonial quarter around the old port and the São José da Amura fortress, rich in history but with limited tourist infrastructure — for history-minded, adventurous travelers.

The city's real center of gravity, lined with government buildings, banks, and most of Bissau's hotels and restaurants around the Presidential Palace — the easiest, most practical base for any visitor.
A calmer, largely residential and commercial district just inland from downtown, favored by NGO staff and longer-stay visitors who want quiet streets close to the center.
A sprawling, densely packed working-class quarter built around West Africa's famous Bandim market — vibrant and authentic, but with almost no visitor amenities.
The corridor along the road to Osvaldo Vieira Airport, increasingly home to newer hotels and aparthotels aimed at business travelers wanting a quick airport run.

water.note: Tap water is not considered safe to drink; use bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: There is no formal ticketing system; pay the driver or tout in cash (CFA francs) on boarding toca-tocas and shared taxis, and agree private taxi fares verbally before the ride since meters aren't used.
transit.hours: Informal daytime service roughly 6am-9pm; little to no scheduled transit after dark, though private taxis can usually be hailed or phoned at night.
transit.note: Bissau has no metro, tram, or formal city bus network — getting around relies on shared minibuses (toca-tocas), shared taxis, and private taxi hire.

bus: Shared bush taxis and minibuses to regional towns (Bafatá, Gabú, Cacheu)
Long-distance routes to Ziguinchor, Senegal and Conakry, Guinea
ferry: Inter-island boats and pirogues from the Port of Bissau to the Bijagós Archipelago (Bubaque, Orango, and other islands)

airport.name: Osvaldo Vieira International Airport (OXB)
rentals: No major international rental chains operate at OXB; hotels and local travel agencies arrange car-with-driver hire

tip.r: Not customary or expected; rounding up the bill or leaving small change at restaurants and for taxi drivers is appreciated but not required.

food.name: Caldo de mancarra
food.desc: Guinea-Bissau's national dish: a thick groundnut stew, usually with shrimp or chicken, spiked with chili and poured over white rice.

places.name: Coqueiros
places.note: One of the liveliest kitchens in the capital and well known for its mancarra and jollof-style rice.

places.name: Por do Sol
places.note: Traditional Bissau-Guinean cooking alongside international plates; strong on the caldos.

places.name: O Bigode
places.note: Simple local favourite where the traditional food is consistently good and cheap.

food.name: Caldo de peixe
food.desc: Fish stew built on tomato, onion, palm oil and chili with whatever came in from the Geba estuary that morning, served over rice.

places.name: Por do Sol
places.note: Specialises in caldo de peixe; the standard recommendation for the dish in Bissau.

places.name: Coqueiros
places.note: Busy dining room turning out fish caldos and estuary seafood all evening.

places.name: Restaurante Papa Loca
places.note: Broad menu of local stews and grills; reliable when other kitchens are quiet.

food.name: Chabeu
food.desc: Fish simmered in a deep-orange sauce of pressed red palm fruit, thick and slightly smoky - the most distinctively Bissau-Guinean thing on any menu.

places.name: Coqueiros
places.note: Serves chabeu the traditional way, with rice to soak up the palm-fruit sauce.

places.name: O Bigode
places.note: Short menu, but this is where locals go for the national stews done plainly.

places.name: Bandim Market cook stalls
places.note: Market cooks ladle chabeu and mancarra from big pots at lunchtime for a couple of dollars.

food.name: Jollof-style rice
food.desc: Rice cooked down in tomato, onion and palm or groundnut oil with fish or chicken buried in it - the everyday one-pot meal across the country.

places.name: Coqueiros
places.note: Named in local guides for its jollof-style rice as well as its groundnut stew.

places.name: Bandim Market cook stalls
places.note: The cheapest and most authentic plates in the city, dished up from morning to mid-afternoon.

places.name: Restaurante Papa Loca
places.note: Sit-down version with a choice of fish or grilled meat on top.

food.name: Grilled fish and prawns
food.desc: Snapper, barracuda or tiger prawns split and charred over coals, dressed with lime and the fierce peri-peri that sits on every table.

places.name: Por do Sol
places.note: Grilled seafood with a view over the estuary; lobster and prawns when in season.

places.name: Bandim Market grills
places.note: Street vendors grilling whole fish over charcoal - point at what you want.

places.name: Coqueiros
places.note: Big charcoal grill and the city's best-known crowd for an evening seafood plate.

food.name: Mangrove oysters
food.desc: Small, intensely salty oysters prised off mangrove roots in the Geba delta, eaten raw with lime or cooked into a peppery soup.

places.name: Por do Sol
places.note: Oyster and crab soups are a house speciality alongside the fish stews.

places.name: Coqueiros
places.note: Serves the estuary oysters in season, grilled or in soup.

places.name: Porto Pidjiguiti waterfront stalls
places.note: Women sell bagged mangrove oysters straight off the boats near the old quay.

food.name: Sumo de caju
food.desc: Juice pressed from the cashew apple - astringent, tropical and unlike anything else. Guinea-Bissau lives on cashews, and this is the fruit half of the crop.

places.name: Bandim Market juice sellers
places.note: Fresh-pressed caju by the bottle during the spring harvest; cheapest in the city.

places.name: Coqueiros
places.note: Keeps chilled cashew and tropical juices on the drinks list year round.

places.name: Mercado de Caracol stalls
places.note: Central-market vendors sell caju juice alongside roasted cashew nuts to take away.

food.name: Bissap
food.desc: Iced hibiscus infusion, deep red and tart-sweet, often scented with mint or ginger - the West African refresher sold on every corner.

places.name: Bandim Market juice sellers
places.note: Sold frozen in small bags as well as poured over ice; ask for the ginger version.

places.name: Mercado de Caracol stalls
places.note: Bissap and gingembre from coolers beside the produce stalls.

places.name: Restaurante Papa Loca
places.note: Serves house-made bissap with meals if you would rather sit down than drink on the street.

landmarks: Fortaleza d'Amura (Fort of Amura)
A star-shaped Portuguese colonial fortress on the waterfront where the remains of independence hero Amílcar Cabral now rest; its weathered ramparts offer sweeping views over the Geba River estuary.
Praça dos Heróis Nacionais (National Heroes Square)
The symbolic heart of the city, this monument-studded square honors the leaders of Guinea-Bissau's independence struggle and is a natural starting point for exploring downtown Bissau.
Bandim Market

A sprawling, chaotic, and colorful open-air market packed with produce, fabrics, and street food, offering an unfiltered slice of everyday Bissau-Guinean life and some of the best people-watching in the country.
Bissau Cathedral (Sé Catedral de Bissau)
A modest but photogenic Portuguese-era Catholic cathedral in the old town, its whitewashed facade standing as a quiet reminder of the city's colonial past.
Pidjiguiti Memorial
A dockside monument marking the 1959 Pidjiguiti dockworkers' strike and massacre, a pivotal spark in the fight for independence from Portugal and an important pilgrimage site for history buffs.
Presidential Palace (Palácio da Presidência)
The imposing, still-scarred former seat of government, damaged during the 1998-99 civil war, makes for a striking architectural and historical photo stop in the city center.
Old Portuguese Colonial Quarter
Wander crumbling pastel-hued Art Deco and colonial buildings lining shaded avenues, a wonderfully atmospheric, slightly faded snapshot of 20th-century Portuguese West Africa.
Bissau Velho (Old Bissau) Waterfront
The original riverside settlement area where fishing pirogues line up along the muddy banks of the Geba, offering an authentic and vibrant maritime scene.
Amílcar Cabral Statue and Mausoleum Grounds
A striking bronze tribute to Guinea-Bissau's founding father and revolutionary theorist, set within the fortress grounds and central to the nation's identity.
Bissau Central Mosque
One of the city's principal mosques, reflecting the significant Muslim population of Guinea-Bissau, with an active, welcoming community atmosphere around its courtyard.

train.note: Guinea-Bissau has never had a railway - no line was ever built in the country and none is planned. The nearest passenger rail of any kind is in Senegal, and even there it now runs only around Dakar. All movement into and out of Bissau is by road, boat or air, so there is no station, operator or timetable to consult.

intl.op: shared seven-seat taxis and minibuses — tickets at the Paragem yard in Bissau, no online booking
shared taxis and minibuses — tickets at the Paragem yard, no online booking

bus.note: Long-distance transport uses the Paragem yard near Bandim market on the northern side of the centre, where shared seven-seat Peugeot taxis and minibuses leave when full, mostly early in the morning. Ziguinchor in Senegal's Casamance is 2.5-3 hours away for around CFA 4,000, with about CFA 1,000 extra charged for a normal-sized bag, and from there you can continue to Dakar or the Gambia. The run to Conakry in Guinea via Gabú and Koundara takes a long, rough day or more and the roads deteriorate badly in the June-October rains. Nothing is bookable in advance - pay cash in CFA francs at the yard - and have visas arranged beforehand, as none of these borders issues one reliably on arrival.

intl.to: Bubaque, Bijagós Islands (Guinea-Bissau) - sails from Porto Pidjiguiti in central Bissau
intl.op: government-run ferry — tickets at the quayside, no online booking

intl.to: Bolama & other Bijagós islands (Guinea-Bissau) - sails from Porto Pidjiguiti
intl.op: local canoa and pirogue operators — arranged at the quayside

ferry.note: Boats leave from Porto Pidjiguiti, the old colonial dock a short walk from the presidential palace in the middle of Bissau. The state ferry to Bubaque, the main island of the Bijagós archipelago, sails only a few times a week and takes roughly five to seven hours; departures are moved or cancelled without notice and no timetable can be relied on from abroad. The alternative is a canoa - a large motorised pirogue - which is cheaper, slower and completely open to the weather, so bring sun cover and expect to get wet. There are no international passenger sailings from Bissau; the port's other traffic is cargo only.

half.name: Ziguinchor
